reading.title: Discussing a cut
reading.text: Mona visits a salon for a trim because she wants to keep most of her length. The stylist compares layers and a bob before confirming her request. At the consultation desk, other style examples include a pixie, fade, undercut, bangs, buzz cut and shag. A guide explains crew cut and mohawk. Bangs/Fringe gives American and British terms for hair across the forehead. At the mirror, Mona asks about a side part, comb over and braids. The stylist uses these names to understand the desired arrangement, not to judge identity, professionalism or character from someone’s hair.

reading.title: Choosing an arrangement
reading.text: Leila discusses an event hairstyle with the stylist. The examples include cornrows, dreadlocks and extensions. She also sees a wig and hair net and asks what a blow dry involves. The stylist explains curl, straighten and braid as actions. Leila compares an updo, ponytail and bun, learning that a bun may be part of an updo. She finally describes waves and asks whether the stylist can twist a section and hold it with a pin. The stylist confirms her wishes before touching her hair. The names help the conversation without assigning styles to a gender, ethnicity or personality.

reading.title: Tools and products
reading.text: Before a service, the stylist explains a tool display. Hair rollers, a curling iron and a flat iron shape hair in different ways. A blow dryer directs air, while a diffuser spreads it. A hair cape protects clothing. A fresh neck strip belongs under a cape, and the barber pole is the sign outside. Shaving cream and aftershave are discussed as grooming products. Pomade, hair gel, hair wax, mousse and hair spray have different textures and purposes. The client learns the names but receives no blade-use, heating or chemical instructions from this vocabulary account.
